newsitem.title: USA: Despite efforts to ban them, chain letters live on.
newsitem.headline: Despite efforts to ban them, chain letters live on.

text.p: Chain letters are rude, illegal -- and all over the Internet.

Whether soliciting money for illegal pyramid schemes or innocently asking people to pass on a little good luck, chain letters have become a fixture in the e-mail inboxes of Internet users that no amount of n'etiquette coaching or threats from access providers can stop.

Judging from the number of chain letters posted to newsgroups or Web sites retelling urban legends or asking people to send loving thoughts to 10 friends, some people are a soft touch for a well-worded electronic appeal.
Internet user Susan Culligan said she doesn't usually go in for chain letters, but after a good-luck totem landed in her e-mail box recently, the loan she'd been waiting for came through.
"This might have happened anyway, but who knows," Culligan said.
Others only find it annoying.

"I don't mean to be cold, but it just doesn't seem right to impose on people's time," said Bert Shankle, a magazine advertising production manager in New York. "It's like panhandling for emotions. If what you're communicating is second hand, let alone on its 15th trip around the world, then I almost surely don't give a hoot."

Because chain letters are unsolicited, they fall into the same category as junk e-mail or "spam," an activity most Internet service providers explicitly forbid in their acceptable use policies or subscriber terms of service.
Internet providers don't police users' e-mail for chain letters. But they do follow up on complaints from subscribers.

In an average week, Pacific Bell Internet Services (http://public.pacbell.net/) receives more than 20 complaints from customers of its California Internet access business about unwanted chain mail. Erols (http://www.erols.com), the Springfield, Va., Internet service provider, suspends or cancels several customers a week because they've been caught sending chain letters asking for money or pitching get-rich-quick schemes, both illegal gambling practices according to U.S. postal codes.
Even sending the more harmless variety of chain letters isn't good online manners, said Mike "Rosie" Hanks, abuse administrator at Erols.
"The net was designed with the assumption that people would behave themselves. But it's clear that, left to their own devices, people don't behave," Hanks said.

N'etiquette isn't the only reason Internet service providers and others try to stomp out chain letters. All that mail can add to traffic on already overtaxed computers that work as Internet mail servers.
For some Internet service providers, the additional burden is nominal.

"It does come up, but it's not in the 'big deal' category," said Glee Cady, public policy manager at Netcom On-Line Communications (http://www.netcom.com, the San Jose, Calif., Internet service provider.

That wasn't the case at the University of Colorado at Boulder (http://www.colorado.edu), where earlier this year a spam-like chain letter sent to thousands of university e-mail addresses nearly shut down the computer network in the school's information technology services department.

According to officials, people who received the message and attempted to reply to the sender inadvertently sent a copy of the reply to everyone else on the list. It created a cascade effect that filled up several hundred megabytes of disk space and took three systems analysts six hours to fix, said Linda Drake, an university computer systems manager.
"It was quite a mess," Drake said.
Some chain letters have become electronic urban legends.

A recent example revolved around Jessica Mydek, a seven-year-old cancer victim whose last request was to start a chain letter reminding people to live life to the fullest. According to the message, the American Cancer Society (http://www.cancer.org) was a corporate sponsor and would donate three cents toward cancer research for every copy of the letter mailed.
Over at least seven months, scores of Internet users complied, posting the request on Web sites and newsgroups from as far away as Germany and Australia.

But the whole thing was a hoax, and in late June, the American Cancer Society posted a warning message on its Web site saying as much and explaining that the organisation never uses chain letters for fund raising.

Another recent chain-letter hoax warned America Online subscribers of a computer virus called AOL4FREE contained in an innocent-looking e-mail message that could destroy a hard drive if it was downloaded.
Experienced Internet users believe electronic chain letters will die down as newcomers learn the rules of the road.

"People think they're doing a good deed by forwarding these, but they're not," said Drake, with the University of Colorado. "I'm sure once everyone is old hat at e-mail, this won't be as much of a problem, but so many new people are coming on and they haven't been exposed to it yet."
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
